ARRAY_LITERAL.documentation: A bracketed list of literals, `['a', 'b']`. Every element must share one type; a numeric array becomes ARRAY<FLOAT64> because the element width is not known at parse time.
ARRAY_LITERAL.notes: Usable as an operand - the right side of `= ANY(...)`, `IN UNNEST(...)`, the array containment operators. It CANNOT be projected: `SELECT ['a','b']` is refused.

BETWEEN.documentation: Inclusive range test. `NOT BETWEEN` is the negation, so its bounds are STRICT and its connective is OR.
BETWEEN.lowering: expr >= low AND expr <= high (negated: expr < low OR expr > high)
BETWEEN.notes: Lowered at build time, so the node renders as the rewrite rather than as the SQL that was written. Any alias must reach the outermost AND/OR node or the column is named after the rewrite.
syntax_forms: expr NOT BETWEEN low AND high

CASE.documentation: Both the searched form (`CASE WHEN cond THEN ...`) and the simple form (`CASE operand WHEN value THEN ...`), which is lowered by comparing the operand to each branch value for equality.
CASE.lowering: simple form: each WHEN value becomes `operand = value`
CASE.notes: ELSE is optional; its absence yields NULL.
syntax_forms: CASE WHEN cond THEN result [WHEN ...] [ELSE result] END
CASE operand WHEN value THEN result [ELSE result] END

CAST.documentation: Type conversion. `TRY_CAST` and `SAFE_CAST` are the non-raising forms - they yield NULL where `CAST` raises.
CAST.notes: A literal operand is converted at plan time. Parameterised targets take their parameters through the cast's parameter channel: `CAST(x AS ARRAY<VARCHAR>)`, `CAST(x AS VECTOR(2))`, `CAST(x AS DECIMAL(p, s))`.

CUBE.documentation: A GROUP BY grouping construct denoting every subset of the keys.
CUBE.notes: Parses - the dialect enables the whole production - but nothing lowers it, so it is refused by name. This is a lowering gap, not a design one: the internal representation (an explicit list of grouping sets) already accommodates it. ROLLUP is the supported construct.

EXISTS.documentation: Tests whether a subquery returns any row. `NOT EXISTS` is supported.
EXISTS.notes: The subquery is embedded as a SUBQUERY parameter and bound in place; the optimizer then decorrelates it. In a SELECT list it ships as a left existence join that emits the verdict.

GROUPING_SETS.documentation: A GROUP BY grouping construct listing the key sets explicitly.
GROUPING_SETS.notes: As CUBE - parses, refused by name, no lowering. ROLLUP is the supported construct.

HEX_LITERAL.notes: Always INT64; this is a number, not a binary string.

INTERVAL.documentation: An interval literal. Units are YEAR, MONTH, DAY, HOUR, MINUTE, SECOND; the compound form spans a contiguous run of them from the leading unit.
INTERVAL.notes: The value is a (months, microseconds) pair - the two components that cannot be reconciled without a calendar. The value must be QUOTED and a leading unit is required. This is the one type-prefixed string literal the dialect still accepts.

IN_LIST.documentation: Membership test against a constant list.
IN_LIST.lowering: the list becomes one ARRAY literal on the right of InList/NotInList
IN_LIST.notes: Every element must be a CONSTANT and they must share one type. Arithmetic elements (`d_year IN (1999, 1999+1)`) are constant-folded at build time; an element that does not fold is refused. The resulting operators are catalogued in operators.json.

IN_SUBQUERY.documentation: Membership test against the rows a subquery returns.
IN_SUBQUERY.notes: A different builder from IN_LIST - the IN-list grammar admits no column references. In a SELECT list it ships as a left existence join.

IN_UNNEST.documentation: Membership test against the elements of an array expression.
IN_UNNEST.notes: The positive form runs. The NEGATED form lowers to AllOpNotEq, which has no kernel, so `NOT IN UNNEST(...)` fails at execution - see the ALL entry.

IS_DISTINCT_FROM.documentation: Null-safe comparison. TOTAL - it never answers UNKNOWN, which is the whole point of the operator: `NULL IS DISTINCT FROM NULL` is FALSE.
IS_DISTINCT_FROM.lowering: (a IS NULL AND b IS NOT NULL) OR (a IS NOT NULL AND b IS NULL) OR (a IS NOT NULL AND b IS NOT NULL AND a != b)
IS_DISTINCT_FROM.notes: The null-test guard around the comparison is load-bearing - drop it and the operator answers UNKNOWN where the standard requires FALSE. The lowering is deliberately built from comparisons, boolean algebra and null tests so the final opcode produces a mask the native filter accepts.
syntax_forms: a IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b

MATCH_AGAINST.documentation: Similarity match of a column against a query string.
MATCH_AGAINST.notes: Matching is by embedding cosine similarity, tuned with `SET match_threshold` - NOT MySQL full-text search. Exactly one column is accepted, and MySQL's search modifiers are refused rather than ignored.

NESTED.notes: Kept as its own node rather than collapsed, because it is the outermost node of a parenthesised select item and so is what carries the alias.

NULL_LITERAL.notes: Typed NULL, so two NULL literals in one select list stay distinct columns.

NUMERIC_LITERAL.notes: An exact integer takes the narrowest native tier that holds it.

PLACEHOLDER.notes: Placeholders are substituted before the plan is built. Reaching this builder means one was left unbound, and it raises - a query is never planned with a hole in it.

QUANTIFIED_ALL.documentation: Comparison that must hold against every element of an array.
QUANTIFIED_ALL.lowering: COMPARISON_OPERATOR named 'AllOp' + the comparison, e.g. AllOpNotEq
QUANTIFIED_ALL.notes: The PATTERN forms run natively (draken_like_any): `LIKE ALL` requires every pattern to match, and `NOT LIKE ALL` requires none of them to - the latter is the De Morgan dual of `LIKE ANY`, NOT the negation of `LIKE ALL`. The COMPARISON forms plan but do not run: the ordering comparisons are rejected as unknown operators, and AllOpEq/AllOpNotEq are rejected as outside the c-native predicate set. `NOT IN UNNEST(...)` lowers here and inherits that gap. The patterns must be bracketed.

QUANTIFIED_ANY.documentation: Comparison that must hold against at least one element of an array.
QUANTIFIED_ANY.lowering: COMPARISON_OPERATOR named 'AnyOp' + the comparison, e.g. AnyOpEq
QUANTIFIED_ANY.notes: The pattern operators take the quantifier too - `name LIKE ANY ('a%', 'b%')` builds AnyOpLike. The patterns must be bracketed. `NOT LIKE ANY` and `NOT ILIKE ANY` are REFUSED: they decompose to `NOT(a AND b)`, which is true unless every pattern matches, and that is almost never what is meant. Write `NOT LIKE ALL (patterns)` for rows matching none of the patterns, or `NOT (LIKE ALL (patterns))` for the literal reading.

ROLLUP.documentation: A GROUP BY grouping construct denoting the prefix hierarchy of its elements, coarsest last: `ROLLUP(a, b)` groups by (a, b), (a) and ().
ROLLUP.lowering: a flat key list plus the grouping-set index tuples the aggregate carries
ROLLUP.notes: The element nesting is load-bearing: `ROLLUP((a, b), c)` has TWO elements, the first composite, and rolls up to three sets, not four. Deliberately not a Node - it describes which sets to group by and only ever appears as a GROUP BY member, so anything else that receives one fails loudly.

SCALAR_SUBQUERY.documentation: A subquery used as an expression value.
SCALAR_SUBQUERY.notes: Stays a subquery through the plan rewriter and is bound in place; the optimizer's decorrelation strategy then removes it, using the binder's resolution of each name to tell a correlated reference from a local one.

SIMILAR_TO.documentation: Refused. SQL-standard pattern match, which Opteryx does not implement.
SIMILAR_TO.notes: REFUSED as of 2026-08-24. SIMILAR TO is its own SQL pattern language - `%` and `_` are the wildcards, `.` is a literal dot - and Opteryx has no implementation of it. It previously parsed and then applied POSIX REGEX to the pattern, which agrees with the standard only by coincidence: `name SIMILAR TO '^C.'` matched C-initial names and would match nothing under the standard. Use RLIKE for regular expressions, LIKE for SQL wildcards. The PostgreSQL regex operators `~` and `!~` were withdrawn at the same time - they were undocumented synonyms for RLIKE / NOT RLIKE, and one spelling per behaviour is the rule. Unary `~` (bitwise NOT) is a different operator and is unaffected.

STRING_LITERAL.notes: A DOUBLE-quoted string is a string literal here, not a quoted identifier. VARCHAR is ASCII bytes.

SUBSCRIPT.documentation: Positional element access on an array-typed expression.
SUBSCRIPT.notes: The subscript must be an INTEGER LITERAL. Field access on a struct uses the arrow operators in operators.json instead.

TUPLE_LITERAL.notes: ALWAYS an ARRAY - a literal is never a VECTOR - so the two literal spellings agree and both reach the ARRAY-typed containment operators. Like the bracket form, it cannot be projected.

TYPED_STRING.notes: Withdrawn - the builder exists only to refuse it by name and point at CAST. INTERVAL is the one prefix literal that remains.
